rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a pitchable question and a fact it does not have. Its "Substack says its top creators made over $400M last year — but won't say who or how much each" is a clean reporter-shaped tension with the missing proof named upfront; B's "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" declares an ad-model story the update never supplied. B has useful bones, but that unsupported contrarian frame is how a founder gets smoked on the first follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is too confident; the update says Substack takes 10% of subscription revenue, not that the cut applies identically to new video or podcast monetization.
"short on funding" overstates the supplied fact, which is only that Substack has had public funding struggles. Good angle, sloppy wording.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" is plausible, but not in the update. A correctly asks for proof later, but the headline frame still imports a cost assumption.
gaps_in_B: "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" invents a key premise. The update gives no ad-policy fact.
"Substack's feed is funded by a 10% cut of paid subscriptions" is not supplied. The facts say there is a 10% subscription cut, not that it funds the feed or excludes other revenue.
"revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" turns one revenue fact into a company-wide cap. That is the kind of overreach a finance reporter will swat down immediately.
"completes a visible identity change from email tool to media app" is too final. The update says Substack has leaned into a media-app strategy; it does not prove the identity change is complete.
